251: Pegler's quote continues: the down-and-out man sees thousands of other people—bookkeepers, clerks, chemists—busy at their work and envies them from the bottom of his soul. They have their independence, their self-respect and manhood, and he simply cannot convince himself that he is a good man too, though he argue it out hour after hour. It is just money which makes this difference. With a little money he would be himself again. Hill then introduces 'The Fear of Criticism.' While no one can state definitely how humanity came by this fear, it is certain people have it in highly developed form. Hill attributes it to that part of inherited human nature which prompts people not only to take away the goods and wares of others but to justify their action by CRITICISM of their victims' character. Thieves criticize those from whom they steal; politicians seek office not by displaying their own virtues but by attempting to besmirch their opponents. The Fear of Criticism takes many forms, mostly petty and trivial. Clothing manufacturers capitalize on this fear by changing styles every season—not the purchaser's idea but the manufacturers', to sell more clothes. Automobile manufacturers do the same, though older models may actually be better cars.
252: Hill examines human behavior when the Fear of Criticism affects more important events. Practically any person reaching mental maturity (35 to 40) would, if you could read their secret thoughts, show a decided disbelief in most fables taught by dogmatists and theologians. Yet few have the courage to openly state their belief. Most people, if pressed, will tell a lie rather than admit they do not believe all stories associated with religion, particularly if their religion is rigidly dogmatic and intolerant. Why does the average person shy away from denying belief in religious dogma that is almost surely fabulous? The answer is 'the Fear of Criticism.' Men and women have been burned at the stake for daring to express disbelief in ghosts. The time was, and not so far in the past, when criticism carried severe punishments—and still does in many countries. The Fear of Criticism robs people of initiative, destroys imagination, limits individuality, takes away self-reliance, and does damage in a hundred other ways. Parents often do irreparable injury by criticizing children. The mother of one of Hill's boyhood chums punished him with a switch almost daily, always completing with 'You'll land in the penitentiary before you are 20.' He was sent to a reformatory at 17. Criticism is the one form of 'service' of which everyone has too much, handed out gratis whether asked for or not. One's nearest relatives are often the worst offenders.
253: Hill states it should be recognized as a crime for any parent to create an inferiority complex in a child through unnecessary criticism. Employers who understand human nature get the best from employees not by criticism but by constructive suggestion. Parents may accomplish the same with children. Criticism will plant FEAR or resentment in the human heart, but it will not build love or affection. Under 'Symptoms of the Fear of Criticism,' Hill notes this fear is almost as universal as the Fear of Poverty, and its effects are just as fatal to personal achievement, mainly because it destroys initiative and discourages the use of imagination. The major symptoms: SELF-CONSCIOUSNESS—nervousness, timidity in conversation and meeting strangers, awkward movements, shifting eyes. LACK OF POISE—lack of voice control, nervousness in presence of others, poor posture, poor memory. WEAK PERSONALITY—lacking firmness of decision, personal charm, ability to express opinions definitely, sidestepping issues, agreeing with others without examining their opinions. INFERIORITY COMPLEX—expressing self-approval to cover up inferiority, using big words to impress, imitating others, boasting of imaginary achievements, sometimes giving a surface appearance of superiority. EXTRAVAGANCE—trying to keep up with the Joneses, spending beyond income. LACK OF INITIATIVE—failure to embrace opportunities, fear to express opinions, lack of confidence in own ideas, evasive answers, hesitancy, deceit.
254: Hill continues symptoms of the Fear of Criticism: LACK OF AMBITION—mental and physical laziness, lack of self-assertion, slowness in reaching decisions, easily influenced by others, criticizing others behind their backs while flattering them to their faces, accepting defeat without protest, quitting when opposed, suspicious without cause, lacking tact, unwilling to accept blame for mistakes. Hill then introduces 'The Fear of Ill Health,' traceable to both physical and social heredity. It is closely associated with causes of the Fear of Old Age and the Fear of Death, leading to the border of terrible worlds about which we have been taught discomforting stories. Certain unethical people engaged in 'selling health' have kept this fear alive. We fear ill health because of terrible pictures planted in our minds of what may happen if death overtakes us, and because of the economic toll it may claim. A reputable physician estimated that 75 percent of all people who visit physicians suffer from hypochondria (imaginary illness). It has been convincingly shown that the fear of disease, even without the slightest cause, often produces the physical symptoms of the disease feared. The human mind is powerful and mighty—it builds or it destroys. Dispensers of patent medicines have reaped fortunes playing upon this common weakness. Colliers' Weekly Magazine conducted a bitter campaign against some of the worst offenders.
255: Hill describes experiments demonstrating that people can be made ill by suggestion alone. Three acquaintances were sent to visit 'victims,' each asking 'What ails you? You look terribly ill.' The first questioner usually provoked a grin and 'Oh, nothing, I'm all right.' The second was answered with 'I don't know exactly, but I do feel badly.' The third was met with frank admission that the victim was actually feeling ill. Hill warns not to carry this experiment too far, as some people may actually develop serious physical symptoms. He mentions a religious sect whose members take vengeance by 'hexing'—placing a spell on victims—and reliable reports exist of individuals dying after being hexed. There is overwhelming evidence that disease sometimes begins in the form of negative thought impulse, passed from one mind to another by suggestion or created in one's own mind. A wise man once said, 'When anyone asks me how I feel, I always want to answer by knocking him down.' Physicians sometimes send patients into new climates because a change of mental attitude is necessary. The seed of Fear of Ill Health lives in every human mind. Worry, fear, discouragement, disappointment in love and business cause this seed to germinate. Hill shares the story of a young man hospitalized after a devastating disappointment in love. A psychotherapist replaced nurses with a charming young woman who showered him with affection by prearrangement. Within three weeks the patient was discharged—HE WAS IN LOVE AGAIN. The remedy was a hoax, but the patient and nurse were later married, both in good health.
256: Hill presents 'Symptoms of the Fear of Ill Health': INAPPROPRIATE AUTOSUGGESTION—negative use of self-suggestion, looking for and expecting symptoms of all kinds of disease, 'enjoying' imaginary illness, trying all fads and 'isms,' dwelling on details of operations and accidents, experimenting with diets and exercise without professional guidance, over-reliance on home remedies and patent medicine. HYPOCHONDRIA—habit of talking about illness, concentrating the mind upon disease, expecting its appearance until a nervous condition occurs. Nothing in bottles can cure this; it is brought on by negative thinking and only positive thought can cure it. Hypochondria is said to do as much damage as the disease one fears. Most so-called cases of nerves come from imaginary illness. LACK OF EXERCISE—fear of ill health interferes with proper physical exercise, results in being overweight by avoiding outdoor life. SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ILLNESS—fear breaks down the body's natural resistance, creates favorable conditions for disease. The Fear of Ill Health is often related to Fear of Poverty, especially in hypochondriacs who constantly worry about doctor's bills and hospital bills, spending time preparing for sickness, talking about death, saving money for cemetery lots and burial expenses. SELF-CODDLING—making a bid for sympathy using imaginary illness as the lure, often to avoid work, feigning illness to cover laziness or lack of ambition.
257: Hill continues symptoms of the Fear of Ill Health: INTEMPERANCE—using alcohol or narcotics to deaden pains instead of eliminating the cause, reading about illness and worrying over the possibility of being stricken, reading or viewing patent medicine advertisements. He then introduces 'The Fear of Loss of Love.' The original source needs little description: on the male side, it grew out of males' early and inherently polygamous nature and propensity to steal the mates of other males. On the female side, it derives from woman's maternal instincts and need for protection during pregnancy and early child nurturing. Both sexes have a biological and behavioral basis to fear loss of love or mate companionship. Jealousy and similar neuroses grow out of this inherited fear. This fear is the most painful of all the Six Basic Fears, playing more havoc with body and mind than any other, and can lead to severe mental problems. The Fear of Loss of Love probably dates back to the Stone Age, when males stole females by brute force. In modern civilization, technique has changed—instead of force, they use the lure of romantic persuasion, promise of fine clothes, expensive automobiles, jewelry, access to economic power, and other bait more effective than physical force. Males' habits are the same as at the dawn of civilization, but expressed differently. Women are generally more susceptible to this fear because through the ages they have learned that men, as a group, are polygamous by nature and not to be trusted in the hands of rivals.
258: Hill presents 'Symptoms of the Fear of Loss of Love': JEALOUSY—being suspicious of friends and loved ones without reasonable evidence, accusing wife or husband of infidelity without grounds, general suspicion of everyone, absolute faith in no one. Jealousy is a form of neurosis which sometimes becomes violent without the slightest cause. FAULT FINDING—finding fault with friends, relatives, business associates, and loved ones upon the slightest provocation or without any cause. GAMBLING—gambling, stealing, cheating, and taking risky chances to provide money for loved ones with the belief that love can be bought, spending beyond one's means or incurring debts to provide gifts for loved ones to make a favorable showing, insomnia, nervousness, lack of persistence, weakness of will, lack of self-control, lack of self-reliance, bad temper. Hill then introduces 'The Fear of Old Age,' which grows out of two sources: first, the thought that old age may bring POVERTY; second, and by far the most common, thoughts arising from false and cruel teachings of the past, mixed with fire and brimstone and 'bogeymen' cunningly designed to enslave people through fear. People have two sound reasons for apprehension: distrust of others who may seize their worldly goods, and terrible pictures of the 'world beyond' planted in their minds through 'social heredity' before they came into full possession of their powers of reason. The possibility of ill health, more common with age, is also a contributing cause. Eroticism enters as well—no one cherishes the thought of diminishing sexual attraction and activity. The most common cause is associated with the possibility of poverty.
259: Hill continues the Fear of Old Age: 'Poorhouse' and everything the term conveys throws a chill into the mind of every person facing the possibility of spending declining years impoverished and worried about meeting both daily necessities and special needs of old age. Another contributing cause is the possibility of loss of freedom and independence—physical and economic. Under 'Symptoms of the Fear of Old Age': THE TENDENCY TO SLOW DOWN and develop an inferiority complex at mental maturity, around age 50, falsely believing oneself to be 'slipping' because of age. (The truth is that one's most useful years, mentally and spiritually, are those between 50 and 60.) THE HABIT OF SPEAKING APOLOGETICALLY of oneself as being old at 60 or 70, instead of expressing gratitude for having reached the age of wisdom and understanding. THE HABIT OF KILLING OFF INITIATIVE, imagination, and self-reliance by falsely believing oneself too old to exercise these qualities. The habit of dressing to appear much younger and affecting mannerisms of youth, thereby inspiring ridicule by both friends and strangers. Hill then introduces 'The Fear of Death'—to some the cruelest of all basic fears. In the majority of cases, the terrible pangs of fear associated with death may be charged directly to religious fanaticism. So-called 'heathen' are less afraid of death than the more civilized. For thousands of years, human beings have been asking the still unanswered questions, 'Whence?' and 'Whither?'—'Where did I come from, and where am I going?'
260: Hill traces the Fear of Death to its major source: during the darker ages, the more cunning and crafty were not slow to offer answers to these questions—FOR A PRICE. 'Come into my tent, embrace my faith, accept my dogmas, and I will give you a ticket that will admit you straightaway into heaven when you die,' cries a leader of sectarianism. 'Remain out of my tent, and may the devil take you and burn you throughout eternity.' ETERNITY is a long time. FIRE is a terrible thing. The thought of eternal punishment by fire not only causes people to fear death, it often causes them to lose their reason, destroying interest in life and making happiness impossible. Hill reviewed a book entitled A Catalogue of the Gods listing 30,000 gods humankind has worshipped through the ages, represented by everything from a crawfish to a man. It is little wonder people have become frightened at the approach of death. While religious leaders may not be able to provide safe conduct into heaven, the possibility of hell seems so terrible that the very thought paralyzes reason and sets up the Fear of Death. In truth, NO ONE KNOWS for certain what heaven or hell is like. This lack of positive knowledge opens the door of people's minds to charlatans who may enter and control those minds with pious fraud and trickery. The fear of DEATH is not as common now as when there were no great colleges and universities. Scientists have turned the spotlight of truth upon the world, rapidly freeing men and women from this terrible fear. Insane asylums have been filled with people who have gone mad because of the FEAR OF DEATH.
